claims.text: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr is a single-phase BCC alloy.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
Replacing Ta with Nb will lower the density of HfMoTaTiZr by approximately 8–10%.
The Nb-substituted alloy will retain 90–100% of the original alloy's room-temperature and approximately 1000 °C mechanical properties.
Induction melting, rapid solidification, and tailored heat treatment can stabilize a single-phase BCC structure in the proposed Nb-substituted HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
Nb has a density of approximately 8.57 g/cm³.
Ta has a density of approximately 16.65 g/cm³.
The lower density of Nb relative to Ta causes Ta-to-Nb substitution to reduce overall alloy density.
Ta-to-Nb substitution will adjust the BCC lattice parameters while retaining substantial lattice distortion.
Retained lattice distortion will provide solid-solution strengthening in the proposed alloy.
Preserving the BCC structure and solid-solution strengthening will preserve mechanical properties at room temperature and approximately 1000 °C.
Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and creep resistance of the modified alloy will remain within 90–100% of the HfMoTaTiZr baseline.
The proposed applicability is limited to room temperature through approximately 1000 °C under tensile loading.
WxNbMoTa alloys with the reported tungsten concentrations form single-phase BCC solid solutions.
Laser-cladding rapid solidification produced approximately 20 μm grains and 4 μm dendrites in WxNbMoTa alloys, smaller than those from vacuum arc melting.
NbMoTa exhibited a reported yield strength of 530 MPa and compressive strain of 8.5% at 1000 °C.
The cited NbMoTa result at 1000 °C was reported to outperform traditional refractory alloys T-111, C103, and Nb-1Zr.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as partial Ta substitution, but the example HfMoNbTiZr removes Ta entirely and therefore represents complete replacement in an equiatomic interpretation.

The hypothesis states that the optimal substitution fraction remains unknown, yet the rejection rule says failure of any tested substitution level falsifies the hypothesis. One nonoptimal composition could therefore reject a hypothesis that only requires some optimized substitution level to succeed.

The boundary is framed only in terms of tensile loading, while creep resistance is also claimed as an outcome without specifying the creep stress, duration, or loading protocol needed to define that boundary.
